header: IN THE LAHORE HIGH COURT, MULTAN BENCH, MULTAN
Province of Punjab through Chief Secretary, Punjab, Lahore & 02 others
Order with signature of Judge and that of parties or
22.06.2026 Mr. Muhammad Hayat Khan, Advocate for petitioner.
body: Asim Juniad, District Accounts Officer, Bhakkar and Khadim Hussain, Camel Breeding and Research Station, Rakh Mahni, Bhakkar.

The brief facts of the instant case are that the petitioner was appointed as Tractor Driver (BS-5) under Rule 17-A of the Punjab Civil Servants (Appointment & Conditions of Service) Rules 1974 (“Rules”) vide order dated 24.07.2024 passed by Superintendent, Camel Breeding & Research Station Rakh Mahni, District Bhakkar. Rule 17-A was omitted from the Rules vide Notification dated 24.07.2024 and the petitioner’s appointment orders were withdrawn in the light of clarification received from S&GAD (Regulation Wing) vide its letter dated 14.10.2024. Feeling aggrieved, the petitioner filed W.P. No. 16942/24 before this Court which, by setting aside the impugned order dated 04.12.2024, was allowed on 08.04.2025 and the competent authority was directed to allow the petitioner to resume his official assignment within 15 days. In compliance of the said order, the appointment order of the petitioner has been restored vide order dated 06.12.2025 passed by Respondent No.2/Superintendent, Camel Breeding & Research Station Rakh Mahni, District Bhakkar and his attendance is being marked and he is performing his duties but his salary is not being released by respondent No.3/District Accounts Officer, Bhakkar. The petitioner through this petition has challenged the action of respondent No.3 of withholding his salaries by claiming the same to be without any legal justification and authority and seeks issuance of direction for release of the same.

2. Respondent No.2 through comments has admitted that petitioner was appointed on 06.12.2025 in compliance of orders dated 08.04.2024 passed by this Court after the ICA No.190 of 2025 and Review Application No. 24 of 2025 in WP No. 16942 of 2024 had been dismissed and the matter had been forwarded to respondent No.3 for release of petitioner’s salary. On the other hand, respondent No.3 has submitted comments to the effect that as amendment in Rule 17-A of the Rules was repealed on 24.07.2024, therefore, the petitioner could not have been appointed on the said date under the same Rule. However, it has not been denied that the repeal of said notification was published on 26.07.2024 i.e. after the date of appointment of the petitioner and the question had arisen that whether the said notification would be applicable from the date of issuance of publication of the same or with retrospective effect.

3. It is not out of place to mention here that in terms of principles laid down in Ayaz Ali and another versus Federation of Pakistan and other (2026 SCMR 42) and Al-Noor Sugar Mills Limited and another versus Federation of Pakistan and others (2018 SCMR 1792), a notification withdrawing any benefit always has a prospective effect and on the basis of said principles the repeal of Rule 17-A on 24.07.2024, which was notified on 26.07.2024, could not be given a retrospective effect to undo the appointment actually made on 24.07.2024, which by then had become past and closed transaction.

4. It would be pertinent to mention here that the matter in issue has already been decided by the Federal Constitutional Court in dispute of similar nature while dealing with cases relating to Rule 11-A of Sindh Civil Servants (Appointment, Promotion & Transfer) Rules, 1974, which is similar in terms to Rule 17-A applicable in Province of Punjab, vide order dated 27.02.2026 passed in FCPLA Nos.508, 591, 346, 347, 348, 589, 267, 593, 130 and 353 of 2025 has held as under:- “The controversy, in the present case, involves the decision of learned Sindh High Court, whereby writ petitions filed by the respondents, were accepted and appropriate direction(s) were made to the petitioner to appoint them on the deceased son/spouse quota.

2. Learned Additional Advocate General, Sindh inter alia contended that in light of the judgment of the Supreme Court of Pakistan reported as General Post Office, Islamabad and others Vs. Muhammad Jalal (PLD 2024 SC 1276), Rule 11-A of Sindh Civil Servants (Appointment, Promotion & Transfer) Rules, 1974 was struck down, hence no appointment can be made on that basis. It was further argued that right in favour of respondents have not culminated inasmuch as the appointment letters had not been issued.

4. As noted above, petitioner is aggrieved of acceptance of writ petitions of the respondents by learned Sindh High Court. The controversy pertains to the fact that respondents are spouse/children of the deceased Sindh civil servants and sought appointments on the basis of Rule 11-A of Sindh Civil Servants (Appointment, Promotion & Transfer) Rules, 1974 (the Rules). The Supreme Court of Pakistan vide judgment passed in case reported as General Post Office, Islamabad and others Vs. Muhammad Jalal (PLD 2024 SC 1276) struck down Rule 11-A ibid and petitioner now seeks benefit thereof on the basis that since the Rule is no longer in the field, no appointment can be made. The nub of the controversy is that at the time when the judgment of the Supreme Court of Pakistan supra was handed down, had the right accrued in favour of the respondents? In this regard, the relevant event, which resulted in the accrual of the right, was the death of the civil servant. As and when the death of a civil servant takes place, one of the children and/or spouse acquires the right to be appointed in the civil service. The process of application and/or a formal appointment letter are administrative acts. Since right had accrued in favour of private respondents, hence judgment of the Supreme Court does not come in their way for appointment on deceased employee children/ spouse quota. It is trite law that judgments of the Supreme Court operate prospectively and not retrospectively. Even-otherwise, the Supreme Court in a subsequent decision clarified that the judgment reported as PLD 2024 SC 1276 supra does not take away the accrued rights and/or set aside the past and closed transactions. In view of above position of law, we do not find any legal infirmity in the reasoning handed down by the learned Sindh High Court, in the impugned judgment, warranting interference.

5. Perusal of afore referred judgment clearly shows that where the candidate whose right to be considered for appointment had matured prior to repeal of law, he would still be considered for appointment despite the fact that Rule 17-A of the Rules had been repealed for the reason that vested right had been accrued in his favour for being considered for appointment under the erstwhile Rule 17-A of the Rules. Even otherwise, the judgment passed by Supreme Court in General Post Office, Islamabad and others Vs. Muhammad Jalal (PLD 2024 S.C. 1276) does not declare the right to be considered for appointment under Rule 17- A of the Rules as void ab initio, hence as the petitioner has been appointed in accordance with the afore-mentioned Rule and the order of recall of his appointment has been set aside by this Court in earlier round of litigation, which has been implemented and the petitioner is performing his duties in furtherance of said orders of reinstatement in service, respondent No.3 has no right to object to his appointment or reinstatement in service and refuse to release his salary.

6. It is important to note here that salary is not a bounty of the state as has been held repeatedly by various courts in Pakistan and, therefore, this Court is competent to issue direction for release of the same. Reliance is placed on principles laid down in Pakistan Through General Manager, P.W.R., Lahore versus Mrs. A. V. Issacs (PLD 1970 SC 415), wherein it has been held as under:

“Upon the view I have taken as regards the applicability of the doctrine of bounty to the case of salary already accrued due under the law prevailing at the time the respondent filed her suit, the respondent's appeal in the High Court was bound to succeed even without invoking in aid the provisions of the Constitution of 1962. The general rule is that the rights of the parties to a suit must be adjudicated upon on the basis of the law prevailing at the date of the institution of the suit. This is what the High Court has done. Its reference to Article 178(3) of the Constitution of 1962 was only for the purpose of pointing out that the makers of the Constitution had expressly included "remuneration" therein as a term and condition of service guaranteed by the Constitution to negative the effect of the decision in the case of Mehrajuddin. I am inclined to agree with this view. Thus sub- Article reads as follows:‑ "178.‑(3) Rules made for the purposes of clause (2) of this Article shall be so framed as to ensure‑ (a) that the terms and conditions of service of a person (in so far as those terms and conditions relate to remuneration or age fixed for superannuation) are not varied to his dis-advantage; and (b) that where an order is made which‑ (i) punishes or formally censures a person; (ii) alters or interprets to the disadvantage of a person any rule affecting his terms or conditions of service; or (iii) terminates the employment of a person otherwise than upon his reaching the age fixed for superannuation, he shall, except where the order is made by the President or a Governor, have at least one appeal against the order and, where the order is made by the President or a Governor, he shall have the right to apply to the President or the Governor for a review of the order."

It seems clear from this that now remuneration is one of the terms of service guaranteed by the Constitution. It cannot be varied to a Government servant's disadvantage. This is thus a guaranteed right. In this view of the matter, it has now set the controversy at rest and sounded the death knell of the bounty theory.”

7. The afore-mentioned principle of law has been reiterated by Superior Court in various judgments, in which it has been held that salary of government servant is no longer "bounty of State" but a guaranteed right and issued a direction for release of the same. Reliance is placed on A. R. Azar versus Pakistan through The Chairman, Railway Board. P.W.R., Lahore and 5 others (1980 PLC (CS) 139 Lahore), Muhammad Nawaz versus Government of Pakistan, through the Secretary Communications and another (PLD 1962 Lahore 443), Iftikhar Ahmad and others versus E.D.O. (Health) (2009 PLC (CS) 600 Lahore), Mst. Hajira Bibi versus Civil Admin Officer, PAF Base, Peshawar and 2 others (2020 PLC (CS) 692 Peshawar) and Zafar Ullah Khan and others versus Federation of Pakistan through Federal Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and 2 others (2025 P L C (C.S.) 1462 Islamabad).

8. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in Mrs. Munawar Sanni versus Director, Army Education (1991 SCMR 135), has held that it was the right of a civil servant to receive salary even by approach to the High Court in constitutional jurisdiction of this Court without having resort to the remedy before the civil court or the Service Tribunal for relief, which was not pertinent in the face of bounden obligation of authorities to satisfy such claim themselves without the necessity of driving a needy litigant from pillar to post.

9. In view of the principles laid down in the aforementioned judgments, respondent No.3 cannot withhold the salary of the petitioner, who is regularly performing his duties, on the ground that being custodian of government exchequer, he is duty bound to follow the Rules and Regulations of Finance Department and the Accountant General of the Punjab, Lahore and the reason for refusal to release salary on account of repeal of Rule 17-A of the Rules is not justified, hence, as long as the petitioner continues to perform duties, his salary shall be timely released. Petition is allowed accordingly. Copy dasti.
